title: Two Sum
interviewTips: Ask if the array is sorted and whether to return indices or values - sorted enables two-pointer, unsorted requires hash map.
Clarify constraints: exactly one solution exists, same element cannot be used twice, and whether duplicates, negatives, or no-solution cases matter.
Discuss trade-off explicitly: brute force uses O(1) extra space but O(n^2) time, while hash map uses O(n) space to achieve O(n) time.
Explain why you check complement before inserting in one-pass hash map to avoid reusing the same element and to handle duplicates like [3,3] correctly.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The most direct first-principles idea is to try every pair. Fix index i, then scan every j greater than i and test if nums[i] + nums[j] equals target. Since exactly one solution exists, the first matching pair must be the answer.
approaches.theory: There are n choose 2 = n*(n-1)/2 unordered pairs with i less than j. Nested loops enumerate all of them without repetition and never use the same element twice by starting j at i+1. Correctness follows by exhaustive search: if a solution pair exists it will eventually be examined. No extra data structure is needed.

timeComplexity.explanation: Double loop checks all n*(n-1)/2 pairs, each check is O(1), so total time is quadratic in n.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only loop indices and a few variables are used, no extra space proportional to input.

steps: return [0,1] immediately without scanning remaining pairs

edgeCases: n=2 minimal input e.g. [1,2] target 3 returns [0,1]
Duplicate values e.g. [3,3] target 6 requires j starting at i+1 so same element is not reused but two equal values at different indices work
Negative numbers and zero e.g. [-1,-2,-3,-4] target -7 or [0,4,3,0] target 0

approaches.name: Approach 2: One-Pass Hash Map
approaches.intuition: Rewrite the equation: for current value x we need y = target - x. As we scan left to right, all values to the left are already known. If we remember them in a hash table mapping value to index, we can check in O(1) whether the needed complement has been seen.
approaches.theory: Maintain map value -> index for elements already visited. At index i, compute complement = target - nums[i]. If complement is in the map, we have found indices map[complement] and i that sum to target. Otherwise insert nums[i] with index i and continue. Checking before inserting guarantees we never reuse the same element. Each element is visited once and each hash operation is O(1) average, giving linear time. Correctness holds because when we reach the second element of the solution pair, the first element is already in the map.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single pass over n elements, each hash table lookup and insert is O(1) average time.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Hash table stores up to n value-to-index entries in the worst case before solution is found.

steps: i=0, num=2, complement=7 not in {} -> store {2:0}
i=1, num=7, complement=2 found in map at index 0 -> return [0,1]

edgeCases: Duplicates with same value e.g. [3,2,4,3] target 6 returns [1,2], and [3,3] target 6 returns [0,1] because check happens before insert
Negative numbers, zeros, and large values work since hash key is exact value, no sorting assumption
Solution at ends e.g. [1,5,3,8,2] target 3 returns [0,4] after map grows to size 4
